An entity is any object, person, place or event about which data is held; its attributes are the data items describing it. Every entity needs a primary key that uniquely identifies each occurrence. The degree of a relationship describes how many occurrences of one entity relate to another: one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many. In crow's foot notation the many end is drawn with three prongs.

In a one-to-many relationship the foreign key goes in the table at the many end. A one-to-one relationship can often be merged into a single table unless the data is optional or needs separate security.

A many-to-many relationship cannot be implemented directly because a field cannot hold a list of values. It is resolved by introducing a link entity whose primary key is usually a composite of the two original primary keys.

Entity?
An object, person, place or event about which data is stored; it becomes a table in a relational database.
Attribute?
A property or characteristic of an entity; it becomes a field in a table.
Primary key?
An attribute, or combination of attributes, that uniquely identifies each record in a table.
Foreign key?
An attribute in one table that is the primary key of another table and is used to link the two tables.
Composite key?
A primary key made up of two or more attributes which together uniquely identify a record.
Link entity?
An entity introduced to resolve a many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many relationships.
